name: Château de Saint Cosme Gigondas Le Claux 2015
text:
## Château de Saint Cosme Gigondas Le Claux 2015

**The story.** [Château de Saint Cosme](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+de+Saint+Cosme,+Gigondas,+France&t=k) sits in a small valley below the jagged limestone peaks of the [Dentelles de Montmirail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dentelles_de_Montmirail) ([see them from above](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Dentelles+de+Montmirail,+Gigondas,+France&t=k)), in [Gigondas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigondas_AOC), about 15 miles (24 km) from [Châteauneuf-du-Pape](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teauneuf-du-Pape,+Vaucluse,+France&t=k). [Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/) calls it the top estate in Gigondas. The Barruol family has been there for centuries. The [estate's own booklet](https://www.saintcosme.com/upload/Booklet_2026_Eng_Page_HD.pdf) says the family acquired it in 1490 and counts fifteen generations of growers; [Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/) says eighteen generations since 1590.

The modern story belongs to Louis Barruol. In 1992 he was 23 and studying for an MBA in Paris when his father Henri, who had run the estate for 35 years, could no longer work after a stroke. Bulk-wine prices had crashed. Louis took over, changed the vineyard work and the ageing, and started bottling the wine himself. He finished his degree by commuting weekly between Paris and Gigondas for a year. Wine Spectator later called him the ["genius of Gigondas"](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/). He added a merchant business in 1997, bought [Château de Rouanne](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Ch%C3%A2teau+de+Rouanne,+Vinsobres,+France&t=k) in [Vinsobres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinsobres_AOC) in 2019, and makes Riesling at [Forge Cellars](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Forge+Cellars,+Burdett,+New+York,+USA&t=k) on [Seneca Lake](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seneca_Lake_%28New_York%29) in New York's [Finger Lakes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Finger_Lakes_AVA) ([estate booklet](https://www.saintcosme.com/upload/Booklet_2026_Eng_Page_HD.pdf)).

**The vineyard: Le Claux.** "Claux" is the old local spelling of "[clos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clos_%28vineyard%29)", from the Latin *clausum*, an enclosed vineyard. It is a 1.8-hectare plot of very old [Grenache](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenache), mixed in with a few other varieties as was the custom. The [estate](https://www.saintcosme.com/upload/Booklet_2026_Eng_Page_HD.pdf) says it appears in the first land registry of 1902 and was probably planted soon after phylloxera, between 1870 and 1880, which makes the vines around 140 to 150 years old. The soil is clay and limestone [marl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marl) from the [Miocene](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miocene) era, with small sharp gravel on top, on an alluvial fan the estate calls the Font des Papes. The estate says Le Claux always gives its most "Burgundian" Gigondas: fine-boned, with sour-cherry aromas. Louis first bottled it separately in 2006 ([Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/)).

Saint Cosme's vineyards face north-northwest, which is unusual and a real advantage in sunny Provence. Louis says they lose two hours of sun every morning while it rises behind the [Dentelles](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Dentelles+de+Montmirail,+Gigondas,+France&t=k). The grapes ripen slowly and are picked in October, weeks after Châteauneuf, with lower sugars and ripe tannins ([Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/)).

**How it's made.** The bunches go into the vat whole, stems and all ([whole-cluster fermentation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Search?search=Whole+cluster+fermentation+wine&go=Go)); Louis has not destemmed since 1994. In the slow-ripening Gigondas climate the stems turn brown by harvest, and he believes they make the wine more elegant and spicy. The wine stays on its skins for about three weeks, with daily pump-overs and a few punch-downs, a technique he learned in [Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burgundy_wine) ([Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/)). Fermentation uses the vineyard's own wild yeasts. The [estate's current sheet](https://www.saintcosme.com/upload/Booklet_2026_Eng_Page_HD.pdf) for Le Claux gives twelve months of ageing in small barrels: 20% new, 50% used once, 30% used twice. The wine is bottled without [fining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clarification_and_stabilization_of_wine) or filtering. The 2015 is 15% alcohol ([iDealwine](https://www.idealwine.com/en/buy-a-wine/2668824-2-bottles-Gigondas-Le-Claux-Saint-Cosme-2015-Red)).

**The vintage.** [John Livingstone-Learmonth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Livingstone-Learmonth), writing for [Decanter](https://www.decanter.com/learn/vintage-guides/rhone-vintage-guides/chateauneuf-du-pape-2015-gigondas-vacqueyras-366743/), called 2015 a generally very good year across the southern Rhône, though not as great as 1990 or 2010. He wrote that the timing of the rain helped the later-ripening areas most. Some Châteauneuf came out "hot", while Gigondas was cool and clear: "a real winner", with fine September weather. He found a cool, sparky, crystalline quality and Burgundy-like finesse in the wines, and expected the best to last 20 to 25 years. Louis Barruol told him 2015 was a major vintage, with the Grenache better than in 2013 or 2014, and the wines fresh rather than hot as in 2003 or 2001. Saint Cosme's plain 2015 Gigondas was named No. 5 in [Wine Spectator's Top 100 of 2017](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/).

**What the critics say for 2015.** Scores as listed by the French merchant [iDealwine](https://www.idealwine.com/en/buy-a-wine/2668824-2-bottles-Gigondas-Le-Claux-Saint-Cosme-2015-Red) (checked on its page):
- **[Wine Spectator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wine_Spectator): 97.**
- **[Decanter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decanter_%28magazine%29): 96.**
- **[James Suckling](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Suckling): 95.**
- **[Vinous](https://vinous.com): 94 to 96** (a barrel score).
- **[Jancis Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jancis_Robinson): 17/20.** On her stricter scale, that is a very good score.
- **[Wine Advocate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wine_Advocate): 92+ on [iDealwine](https://www.idealwine.com/en/buy-a-wine/2668824-2-bottles-Gigondas-Le-Claux-Saint-Cosme-2015-Red).** Other merchants' listings appear to show a higher barrel score, but I couldn't open them, so treat the Advocate number as unsettled. The earlier note on this wine ("Parker score unclear") had found the same problem.
- **[CellarTracker](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CellarTracker) community: 93.6** (from your CellarTracker list).

[iDealwine](https://www.idealwine.com/en/buy-a-wine/2668824-2-bottles-Gigondas-Le-Claux-Saint-Cosme-2015-Red) describes the wine as the domaine's most Burgundian: refined and fresh, with fresh fruit, flowers and oriental spices, and a long life ahead. I couldn't read the full critics' notes for this vintage, so this summary rests on the scores and the estate's own description.

**How it's drinking now.** In October 2026 the wine is eleven years old. Your CellarTracker list gives a window of 2019 to 2030, while [Livingstone-Learmonth](https://www.decanter.com/learn/vintage-guides/rhone-vintage-guides/chateauneuf-du-pape-2015-gigondas-vacqueyras-366743/) expected top 2015 Gigondas to last 20 to 25 years. It should be in its prime now, with the primary fruit softening into leather, dried herbs and spice, and no rush to drink it. Louis Barruol [writes](https://www.saintcosme.com/upload/Booklet_2026_Eng_Page_HD.pdf) that patience is often rewarded: Saint Cosme's lean, tannic 1988 is now, he says, probably the finest wine you can taste there.

**Serving.** Because the wine is unfiltered and over ten years old, expect some sediment. Stand the bottle upright for a day, then [decant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decantation) it about an hour before dinner, leaving the last centimetre behind. Serve it at about 16 to 17°C, a little below room temperature, in a large Burgundy-style glass that suits its finesse.

**Food.** Louis Barruol [writes](https://www.saintcosme.com/upload/Booklet_2026_Eng_Page_HD.pdf) that red wine without food is "inconceivable". [Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/) suggests lamb kebabs with an [Israeli couscous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israeli_couscous) salad for southern Rhône reds like this. My picks: roast lamb with [herbes de Provence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbes_de_Provence), grilled duck breast, a mushroom or truffle [risotto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Risotto), or an aged [Comté](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comt%C3%A9_cheese). I'd avoid very spicy dishes and sweet sauces, which would clash with the alcohol and the dry tannins.

**Value and where to buy.** The 2015 is now found mainly at auction. In the latest store lists on this site, BC Liquor carries Le Claux 2021 at $205.99, and the plain Saint Cosme Gigondas 2023 at $86.99. In France, [iDealwine](https://www.idealwine.com/en/buy-a-wine/2668824-2-bottles-Gigondas-Le-Claux-Saint-Cosme-2015-Red) sells the 2023 Le Claux at about €100. So a 2015 bought at release and aged well is a very good bottle to own.

**From the history books**
- **A Roman holiday town.** Gigondas takes its name from the Latin *Jocunditas*, meaning joy or pleasure. It was founded as a place of rest for veterans of the Roman Second Legion, and a carved head of [Bacchus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dionysus) found there suggests wine was already made ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigondas_AOC)). Retired legionnaires built villas on the hillsides and planted vines and olives ([Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/)). The Roman writer [Pliny the Younger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pliny_the_Younger) travelled these hillsides on his way to [Vaison](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Vaison-la-Romaine,+Vaucluse,+France&t=k) and described their vines ([estate booklet](https://www.saintcosme.com/upload/Booklet_2026_Eng_Page_HD.pdf)).
- **Roman vats under the house.** Louis Barruol has found 25 fermentation vats carved into the rock beneath the château, linked by small channels so the Romans could move wine by gravity. Part of the cellar dates from around 100 AD. He has also dug up a 5,000-year-old stone axe in one of the vineyards ([Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/)).
- **A prince's vineyard.** Gigondas belonged to the [Principality of Orange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principality_of_Orange), which only became part of France in 1703. In 1480 [John of Chalon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_IV_of_Chalon-Arlay), Prince of Orange and an ancestor of the Dutch royal [House of Orange-Nassau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Orange-Nassau), sold land for vines on the Saint Cosme hillside. In 1490 the family's ancestor Esprit Vaton acquired it ([estate booklet](https://www.saintcosme.com/upload/Booklet_2026_Eng_Page_HD.pdf)).
- **The chapel on the label.** Above the vineyards stands the [Romanesque](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanesque_architecture) [chapel](https://www.google.com/maps?q=Chapelle+Saint-Cosme,+Gigondas,+France&t=k) of [Saints Côme and Damien](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cosmas_and_Damian), two early Christian doctors, built in the 11th or 12th century. The family restored it in 1927 and again in the 1970s. Henri Barruol drew the sketch of it that appears on the labels ([Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/)).
- **Saved by a war.** Le Claux was due to be pulled out in 1914 because it gave so little wine. Then the men went to [war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I). [Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/) reports that three brothers who wanted to uproot it all died in the First World War; the [estate's booklet](https://www.saintcosme.com/upload/Booklet_2026_Eng_Page_HD.pdf) says the grandmother lost two brothers. Either way, the estate passed to a sister who kept the old vines. In 1949 Louis's grandfather was killed, and hired managers robbed the family until 1957, when a young furniture maker, Henri Barruol, married the daughter, Claude, and threw them out. The estate says Henri took over Le Claux in 1958, "in a pitiful state", and nursed it back with sheep manure, sweat and love.
- **Gigondas finds its name.** Gigondas won a gold medal in Paris as early as 1894, but until the Second World War most of its wine went to strengthen thin Burgundies. The bitter winter of 1956 killed the [olive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olive) trees, and vines replaced many of them. In 1971 Gigondas left the [Côtes du Rhône](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C%C3%B4tes_du_Rh%C3%B4ne_AOC) Villages and became an appellation in its own right. White Gigondas has been allowed only since 2022 ([Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gigondas_AOC)).

**Curious details**
- **A soil shared with Barolo.** Saint Cosme's Le Poste vineyard, just uphill from Le Claux, grows on [Tortonian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tortonian) marl laid down about 11 million years ago. Louis says it is the only place it surfaces in the Rhône; the next example is in [Barolo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barolo) and [Barbaresco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barbaresco). He often tastes a salty, sea-like note in his wines, and a friend from Barbaresco tastes the same in his ([Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/)).
- **Cello and rugby.** Louis plays the cello and played on a local rugby team ([Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/)).
- **A monk's advice.** The [estate](https://www.saintcosme.com/upload/Booklet_2026_Eng_Page_HD.pdf) likes to quote [Saint Bernard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_of_Clairvaux), who never banned wine for his [Cistercian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cistercians) monks but gave them the rule *moderate bibendum est*: drink in moderation.
- **A wine named for a son.** Louis makes a [solera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solera) wine, "Little James' Basket Press", named after his son, blending each new vintage with older ones going back to 1999 ([Wine Spectator](https://top100.winespectator.com/2017/article/genius-of-gigondas/)).
